items.item: logical replication is named in contrast to physical replication, which uses exact block addresses and byte-by-byte replication
logical replication is used for replicating between different major versions of PostgreSQL
logical replication is used for replicating between PostgreSQL instances on different platforms
replication slots ensure the primary doesn't remove WAL segments until received by all standbys, and doesn't remove rows that could cause a recovery conflict
replication slots can cause the server to retain so many WAL segments that they fill up the space allocated for pg_wal

at.step: Reveal: the outage, and the fix, measured

items.item: PostgreSQL 17 enables the failover of logical slots
PostgreSQL 17 adds sync_replication_slots to enable failover logical slot synchronization
with row-based logging, DML statements aren't logged; each row a statement inserts, updates or deletes is logged separately

Physical and logical replication aren't competing for the same job — physical replication's whole value is being an exact, byte-identical copy (so it can't cross versions), while logical replication's whole value is being a selective, decoded copy (so it can cross versions, but can never be byte-identical).

A replication slot doesn't ship anything itself — it's a promise the primary keeps about what it won't delete yet, which is exactly why the same mechanism (and the same risk) applies to a physical slot and a logical slot alike.

This topic's own measured experiment uses a physical slot specifically because this sandbox's server can't be restarted to enable logical replication — but the retained-WAL number it measures is the identical mechanism a stalled logical slot would trigger, not an approximation of a different one.

The WAL-retention outage this topic measures isn't a logical-replication-specific bug — it's the necessary cost of the exact guarantee a slot provides: the primary genuinely cannot know how much WAL a stalled consumer still needs, so its only safe choice is to keep all of it.

at.step: Reveal: the outage, and the fix, measured

items.item: Before PostgreSQL 17's failover-safe logical slots, a promoted replica had no memory of a logical subscriber's own progress — the subscriber had to be rebuilt from scratch after a failover, which is exactly the gap this feature closes.

Row-based binlog logging and logical replication's own decoded-changes approach solve the same underlying problem from opposite directions: Postgres decodes WAL after the fact into row changes, while row-based MySQL/MariaDB logging records row changes directly instead of ever logging the original statement.

Change-data-capture tooling (Debezium and similar) exists specifically because logical replication's own decoded row changes are exactly the input CDC needs — this topic's own clause naming CDC isn't a tangent, it's naming logical replication's actual real-world use beyond replica databases.

A stalled consumer and a slow consumer create the identical risk at different speeds — this topic measures the stalled (zero-progress) case directly because it is the clean, reproducible extreme; a merely lagging consumer is exactly the subject of the next topic.

'Advancing' a slot isn't the same operation a real consumer performs — a real logical subscriber advances its own slot only as a side effect of actually having read and applied the changes, so forcibly advancing a slot without consuming (as this topic's own experiment does, deliberately, to demonstrate the mechanism) would silently discard data for a real logical replica.

This topic's own 'Prove it' scenario has a two-part answer: the stalled slot keeps retaining WAL regardless of why the consumer is down, and fixing the consumer alone only stops further growth — it doesn't shrink what's already been retained until the consumer actually catches up to the current position.
